info.bio:
Robert Leroy Johnson (Hazlehurst, Misisipi, 8 de mayo de 1911 - Greenwood, Misisipi, 16 de agosto de 1938) fue un cantante, compositor y guitarrista de blues estadounidense. Es considerado uno de los más grandes intérpretes de blues de toda la historia, a pesar de su temprana muerte, a los 27 años, y de haber dejado grabadas sólo 29 canciones.

Después de varios años actuando por todo el sur de los Estados Unidos, tuvo la oportunidad de dejar registradas sus 29 legendarias canciones.

scenes.name: Country blues
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: La cara liberadora y dionisíaca del ritmo africano: un medio para expresar dolor, opresión y deseo sin autocompasión, con un efecto catártico comparable al de la tragedia. Lo conocemos por grabaciones a partir de los años veinte. Forma de doce compases (tónica, dominante, subdominante) con blue notes que oscilan entre tercera mayor y menor, y estrofa AAB; pero los cantantes del campo alargan o acortan los compases a su antojo porque cantan solos con su guitarra. Charlie Patton, más antiguo y ligado a la plantación, dialoga con su guitarra; Blind Lemon Jefferson canta agudo y fino en Texas; Leadbelly, descubierto en una cárcel por los Lomax, acaba en Nueva York; Robert Johnson, tardío y casi desconocido en vida, se convierte en el paradigma del Delta. Gioia duda del origen en los griots africanos: el blues es un tipo de canción nuevo, nacido en el Sur.

podcast.title: Crossroads Legend
podcast.body: In the 1930s, Robert Johnson was repeatedly told to go away by other guitarists because he wasn't good enough. When he returned just months later, he was a master, doing things no one else had thought of. This led to the story that he sold his soul to the devil at a crossroads near Clarksdale, Mississippi (highways 49 and 61) in exchange for guitar virtuosity, a site still visited by people today. "So the story became that Robert Johnson met at a crossroads in rural Mississippi, where he sold his soul to the devil in exchange for guitar virtuosity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Crossroads Myth Origin
podcast.body: The popular myth of Johnson selling his soul to the devil at a crossroads for guitar skills was originally associated with a different Mississippi bluesman, Tommy Johnson, and there's no contemporary evidence it was believed about Robert Johnson. "Though that's a myth that was originally told about a different Mississippi blues man, called Tommy Johnson, and there's no evidence that anyone thought that of him at the time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Diverse Musical Tastes
podcast.body: Ramblin' Johnny Shines, who traveled with Johnson, reported that Johnson enjoyed playing a variety of songs including "Yes Sir That's My Baby," Jimmie Rodgers songs, and polkas, even calling him a "polka-hound man." "Ramblin Johnny Shines, who travelled with Johnson for a time, described him as particularly enjoying playing songs like Yes Sir That's My Baby, and Jimmy Rogers songs, and Polkas, calling Johnson a polka-hound man."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Dylan's Realistic Perception
podcast.body: In his autobiography "Chronicles," Bob Dylan described Johnson as a "bothersome kid who played harmonica," later learning guitar from records rather than live performers, a portrayal closer to reality than the prevailing legend. Dylan was delighted to later learn Johnson's guitar teacher was named Hank Zimmerman. "Dylan's version of Johnson is closer to the reality, as far as we know it, than the Johnson of legend is, and Dylan seems to have been delighted when he found out much later that the name of the musician who taught Johnson to play guitar was Hank Zimmerman."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Forgotten Before Reissue
podcast.body: For the 23 years between his death and the release of "King of the Delta Blues Singers," most blues musicians and listeners would not have recognized Robert Johnson's name, possibly confusing him with the much more famous Lonnie Johnson. "if you'd asked most blues musicians or listeners about Robert Johnson in the 23 years between his death and the King of the Delta Blues singers album coming out. Most of them would have looked at you blankly, or maybe asked if you meant Lonnie Johnson"

podcast.title: Inspiration for Danko Jones' Look
podcast.body: This legendary blues artist served as a direct inspiration for the Toronto band Danko Jones's formal black attire and overall visual style, highlighting his enduring influence on modern musicians. "They were inspired by blues legend Robert Johnson, and a punk band called Nation of Ulysses."

podcast.title: Limited Commercial Success
podcast.body: In his lifetime, Robert Johnson's best-selling record sold approximately 5,000 copies, a very modest number that does not align with his later legendary status. "In his lifetime, his best selling record sold around 5,000 copies"

podcast.title: Missed Spirituals to Swing Concerts
podcast.body: John Hammond wanted Johnson to perform at the 1938 "Spirituals to Swing" concerts but discovered Johnson had died shortly before. Big Bill Broonzy played in his place. "Hammond had wanted to get Johnson to perform at the spirituals to swing concerts, only to find that Johnson had died only a short time earlier."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Mythology vs. Reality
podcast.body: Johnson is widely perceived as the most important and influential blues musician of his generation, influencing blues and R&B, but this is a popular myth. He was influential on white musicians in the 1960s, but not on black musicians in the 1930s, 40s, and 50s. His lifetime best-selling record sold only around 5,000 copies. "There's a popular perception that Johnson was the most important blues musician of his generation, and that he was hugely influential on the development of blues and album B, and it simply falls."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Post-Mortem Reputation Explosion
podcast.body: Robert Johnson was known by myths and legends among hardcore Delta Blues fans while he was alive, but his reputation exploded in 1961 when his records were reissued, 23 years after his death. "Not when you anything about Robert Johnson when he was alive, other than some myths and legends among hardcore fans of Delta Blues, but when his records were reissued in 1961, 23 years after he died, his reputation exploded."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Remarkable Musical Mind
podcast.body: Despite the myths, Johnson was a truly great musician, a versatile and skilled guitarist and arranger with a broader musical palette than his recorded legacy suggests. "While the myth of Robert Johnson has almost no connection to the real man, his music demonstrated a remarkable musical mind."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Sparse Lyrical Style
podcast.body: Johnson possessed a sparse, economical lyrical style that deeply resonated with Bob Dylan on a primal level. "Johnson had a very sparse, economical, living style, which connected with Dylan on a primordial level."

xref.title: Diverse Musical Inspirations
xref.body: His inspirations include Jimi Hendrix, Joe Strummer, Captain Beefheart, Frank Zappa, Robert Johnson, Bernard Sumner of New Order, and significantly, John McGeoch of Siouxsie and the Banshees, admired for his varied soundscapes. "And who does he look for for inspiration? Well, we talked about Hendrix, but also Joe Strummer, Captain B. Fart, Frank Zappa, loose legend Robert Johnson, Bernard Sumner of New Order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formal Black Attire and Shoe Polish Ritual
xref.body: The Toronto-based band Danko Jones is characterized by its members' exclusive use of black attire, a style inspired by blues legend Robert Johnson and the punk band Nation of Ulysses. Prior to every gig, they meticulously press their clothes to ensure a formal appearance, and no tour can commence without a full supply of shoe polish, underscoring their commitment to this sharp, polished image. "Dango Jones, the Toronto band is all about dressing in black. They were inspired by blues legend Robert Johnson, and a punk band called Nation of Ulysses. They pressed their clothes before every gig to make sure they got that formal look. And no Dango Jones tour is ready to start with a full supply of shoe polish."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Frankenmuth Hometown and Musical Upbringing
xref.body: The Kiszka brothers grew up in Frankenmuth, central Michigan, a town of approximately 5,000 residents whose main attraction is the "world's largest Christmas store." Their parents exposed them to classic rock and blues music, including artists like Led Zeppelin, Jimi Hendrix, Joni Mitchell, and 30s/40s folk and blues legends like Muddy Waters and Robert Johnson. "They're really from the middle of nowhere, a central Michigan town called Frankenmuth. In about 5,000, the biggest attraction is the self-proclaimed world's largest Christmas store. This is where the Kiska family grew up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for Danko Jones' Look
xref.body: This punk band was a direct inspiration for the Toronto-based band Danko Jones's formal black attire and overall visual style, demonstrating their impact on contemporary punk and rock aesthetics. "They were inspired by blues legend Robert Johnson, and a punk band called Nation of Ulysses."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nurturing Musical Environment
xref.body: The Kiszka brothers were raised in a "musically nurturing environment" that extended beyond just music to include film and literature. They were surrounded by traditional music, including early American blues artists like Elmore James, Willie Dixon, Robert Johnson, Muddy Waters, and Howlin' Wolf, as well as folk artists like Arlo Guthrie, Bob Dylan, Joni Mitchell, and John Denver, primarily from their parents' vinyl collection. "we were kind of raised in a musically nurturing environment where it wasn't necessarily just music, but there was a lot of film and a lot of literature. And we had a lot of traditional music, you know, lying around."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
